name: Grande Armee corps system (1805-1812)

weightNotes.aggression: Napoleon sought the decisive battle against the main enemy army in every campaign 1805-1812 (Ulm, Austerlitz, Jena, Friedland, Wagram, Borodino); Chandler, Campaigns of Napoleon, parts 7-12.
weightNotes.maneuver: Manoeuvre sur les derrieres: Ulm 1805 forced Mack's surrender with little fighting, Jena 1806 placed the army across the Prussian line of retreat (Chandler parts 7-8). Kept below 1 because 1809-1812 battles (Aspern, Wagram, Borodino) became attritional slugging matches.
weightNotes.flanking: Corps marching on parallel routes converged on the enemy flank and rear (Davout at Auerstedt, Ney at Friedland, Davout's flank march at Austerlitz); Chandler parts 7-9.
weightNotes.siegePreference: The objective was the enemy field army, not fortresses; sieges (Danzig 1807, Saragossa 1808-09) were delegated to secondary forces. Capitals were taken after the field army was beaten (Vienna 1805, Berlin 1806).
weightNotes.reserveUse: Guard and Cavalry Reserve held back for the decisive blow (Austerlitz, Wagram); Napoleon's refusal to commit the Guard at Borodino shows the habit. Most corps strength was committed, so the held-back fraction is low-moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Light cavalry screens of each corps plus the Cavalry Reserve gave good operational intelligence in 1805; in 1806 Napoleon misplaced the main Prussian army (fought the smaller part at Jena), and in 1812 the cavalry wore out its horses early. Moderate-good.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.napoleonic high quartile 0.333 (1789-1849 rule). Sourced holding: corps were built to hold an army for a day (Everson on Lannes; Chandler). Auerstedt 1806: Davout's III Corps lost 7,052 of 26,000, about 27%, and held and won (Auerstedt page), so its threshold lies above 0.27.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Each corps d'armee had infantry divisions, its own light cavalry, artillery and engineers and fought as a combined-arms unit (Everson, DTIC ADA284591). Grand batteries (Friedland, Wagram, Borodino) integrated artillery with assault.
weightNotes.initiative: Marshals ran their corps independently on the march and in the opening battle (ADA284591), but operational direction was entirely Napoleon's; marshals did poorly when left without him (Spain 1808-1812). Mid value.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Armies lived largely off the country and outran magazines; this worked in rich central Europe and failed in Poland 1807 and Russia 1812 (Jelinek, DTIC AD1022125).

summary: Napoleon split the army into permanent corps of 15,000-40,000 men, each a small army of all arms able to fight alone for a day. Corps marched dispersed on parallel roads within a day or two of each other ('march divided, fight united'), screened by light cavalry, and concentrated on the battlefield or on the enemy's line of communication. One corps fixed the enemy while others came in on the flank and rear; the Guard and Cavalry Reserve delivered or exploited the decisive blow, often after a grand battery had opened a gap. Supply relied on requisition and foraging plus short-lived depots, which bought speed. Conscription (Jourdan law 1798) fed replacements on a scale ancien-regime armies could not match.
whyItWorked: Dispersed marching gave speed and let the army feed itself, while each corps' ability to hold for a day meant concentration could happen on the battlefield itself. Opponents still marched as single slow armies tied to magazines and were outmanoeuvred before they could concentrate: Ulm 1805 captured an Austrian army with almost no battle, Jena-Auerstedt 1806 destroyed the Prussian field army in one day.
whereItFailed: Eylau 1807 (winter, poor roads and starving troops produced a bloody draw); Spain 1808-1812, where marshals without central direction and a guerrilla war defeated foraging logistics; Aspern-Essling 1809, a failed river crossing; Russia 1812, where foraging collapsed over vast poor country, horses and men died before Moscow, the Russians traded space and avoided encirclement, and Borodino became a frontal battle of attrition. The army of over 600,000 that crossed the Niemen came back with a small fraction.

sources.title: Everson, Marshal Jean Lannes in the Battles of Saalfeld, Pultusk, and Friedland 1806-1807 (CGSC thesis, DTIC ADA284591)

Chandler, The Campaigns of Napoleon (Macmillan), parts 7-12
